newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian oil export staff say on work to rule.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian oil export staff say on work to rule.

text.p: Staff at the Department of Petroleum Resources (DPR) which processes export documents for Nigerian oil shipments have begun a work-to-rule action to back demands for salary payments, a staff spokesman said on Tuesday.
"We are going to work but we are not working until our demands are met," Victor Ajakaye, chairman of the DPR chapter of the white-collar oil workers' union PENGASSAN told Reuters.
The work-to-rule action commenced on Monday and followed the expiration last Friday of the workers' ultimatum to the oil ministry and is the latest blow to hit the Nigerian oil sector.

Nigerian oil buyers have been given notice of delay in exports of about 450,000 barrels per day of Bonny since Monday because of a strike by staff of an oil services firm that handles the berthing and loading of tankers. Nigeria's operating partner in the Bonny fields Royal Dutch/Shell said so far it was not expecting to have to cancel shipments from Bonny.
Ajakaye said salary arrears and other benefits owed the 3,000-strong DPR staff amounted to 300 million naira.
"If DPR operations are not to be grounded then the ministry of petroleum resources must attend to our grievances," he said.
DPR staff are responsible for processing documents before crude oil is lifted from Nigerian terminals.
In February they threatened to go on strike over non-payment of salaries but called it off after part of the wages was paid.
Oil industry sources said the work-to-rule action would slow processing of exports if it was not checked soon.
Nigerian oil officials said oil minister Dan Etete had sent an urgent request for funds from the finance ministry to pay the DPR staff.

DPR staff have generally been unhappy since last summer when the Nigerian military government contracted outside inspectors to check oil shipments following allegations of overloading tankers to rob the government of oil revenues.

But the oil unions have been powerless to force a showdown since 1994 when the military government sacked and detained their key leaders because of a two-month strike in support of presidential claimant Moshood Abiola.

Their current work-to-rule action falls short of the kind of outright strike they embarked on in 1994, which angered the government because it grounded the oil industry that provides the bulk of Nigeria's export income.
